summary: The answer comes from the three May-issue Table MQ-1 'Treasury Bills' quotations (April 28 1972, April 30 1973, April 30 1974). You filter 13-week bills by issue date (February to April), count those above the threshold, and take the geometric mean of the qualifying amounts. a read the raw rows, listed each year's February to April issue dates explicitly, applied a strict '>' threshold, and computed both geometric-mean readings in calc before choosing the one that matched the wording. b misread the stitched column mapping and concluded the April tables held no February to April 13-week issues. It then spent about 70 steps and more than 3 minutes in the PDO-3 new-money issuance tables before coming back to MQ-1. At that point it simply took every 13-week row of each April table. That matches the February to April window in 1972 and 1973, but the 1974 table starts with a bill issued at the end of January, so b's count had one extra bill and its geometric mean shifted. The submit gate raised two provenance findings unrelated to this error. b kept its answer both times. c (T=1.0) matched a.

first_divergence.where: b items 19-22 (show_table --stitch labels shifted; b reads the 26-week issue-date column as the 13-week one and concludes no February to April issues are listed), 24-93 (detour through PDO-3 issuance tables), 41 and 95 (final value list takes all 13-week rows per year, including the 1974 row issued 1/31/74)
first_divergence.what_b_did: Never applied the issue-date filter row by row. After the detour it treated the full 13-week block of each April table as 'issued February to April', which pulled in the 1974 bill issued on the last day of January.
first_divergence.what_a_did: Read raw rows via officeqa docs.read (items 23, 25) and wrote out each year's February to April issue dates (item 26), which excluded the January-issued 1974 bill. It then applied the strict threshold and computed the count and geometric mean in calc (item 28).

seed_text_effect.which_advice: check that the period of each cell you use is the one the question asks for
seed_text_effect.evidence: a item 26 lists the issue date of every candidate row per year before filtering, and a item 28 computes both plausible geometric means ('Alternatives' advice) and then weighs them against the wording (item 29). a also tried printings on MQ-1 (item 30) per the seed. It never cites the seed, and the date listing is natural behaviour, so the causal link is weak.

mechanism_effect.workflow_cost: Neither finding touched the actual error, since no rule checks whether counted rows fall inside the question's date window. flagged_cells bound one input literal to a repaired ROWSPLIT row of a different table (PDO-3 in the 1973_06 issue) rather than the MQ-1 cell b used. That is a value-literal provenance mis-attribution, and b answered it with a printings call on PDO-3. grounded fired on a value b had seen only in truncated output, and b printed the raw line. Two Keep rounds cost about 30 s, and the final 'recorded (kept)' worked as a false confirmation. Before submitting, b also planned to use the gate as an oracle (item 41: 'We can use submit to test. harness gives finding if wrong'), a reading the Accept/Keep text invites. The main cost was the pre-submit detour: 50 requests / 319 s vs a's 13 / 93 s.

tools_usage.a: find_tables ('security market quotations', '13-week bills' found MQ-1), show_table --long (column mislabels noticed), officeqa.py docs.read for raw rows (decisive), calc computing count and both geometric-mean readings in one script, and printings attempted on MQ-1 (no match because rows are keyed by date cells, not labels).
tools_usage.b: find_tables and rg over the corpus, show_table --stitch (shifted headers misled it), many sed raw reads of PDO-3 across six to nine issues, printings on PDO-3 (only to answer the gate), calc with a hand-typed value list, and submit x3 (two Keeps).

lesson: Gate rules cover provenance, vintage and format, not whether each row in a count or aggregate satisfies the question's filter, which is where b failed. A cheap mechanism would require the actor to submit the list of included rows with their filter key (issue date) and check it against the stated window. Binding inputs to cells by literal value alone is ambiguous in tables full of near-identical numbers: here it attached a finding to a row of a different table, prompting a pointless verification round. The Accept/Keep framing also invited b to treat submit as an oracle. show_table --stitch mislabelled the MQ-1 columns (issue date vs amount), which made b doubt the right table. Better header repair for MQ-1-style multi-panel tables, or a warning to read raw rows when a date column's label is suspect, would have avoided the detour.
